newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Mass Belgian rally denounces judicial system.
newsitem.headline: Mass Belgian rally denounces judicial system.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of Belgians marched through Brussels to voice their anger at a judicial system seen as corrupt and a political class marked by self-interest and hesitant to bring about change.

The rally reflected the depth of feelings which have swept the country since a lurid tale of child kidnapping, sex abuse and murder exploded in August. "Ashamed to be Belgian" read one marcher's banner.
"This demonstration was a supreme expression of the people's views," said one analyst on VTM television, describing Sunday's march by 250,000 to 325,000 as a political force not be ignored.

Led by the parents and relatives of missing or dead children, suspected to be victims of a child sex gang, a tide of people wearing or carrying white -- the colour of hope -- swept down a boulevard in the centre of the capital.

Many marchers, of all ages and walks of life, were demonstrating for the first time, expressing their concerns over a law and order system seen as unable to protect ordinary people, and their children in particular, from crime.
The protest gained mass appeal after Belgium's top court removed a popular magistrate from investigations into the paedophile ring alleged to have been led by Marc Dutroux.

Dutroux, a convicted child rapist released 10 years early in 1992 from a 13-year sentence for multiple child rape, is one of 13 people charged in connection with the case in which scores of videos of child pornography were seized.

Spontaneous protests broke out across Belgium after the court ruled that magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte compromised himself by accepting a free dinner from a support group specialising in helping the parents of missing children.
The ruling, following the letter rather than the spirit of the law, prompted an already morally-outraged public to take to the streets and call for a clean-up of the justice system.
The march was mainly silent in line with the wishes of the parents of four girls whose bodies were unearthed in mid-August after Dutroux told police where to look.

Gerda Zammattio, who brought her three-year-old daughter from the town of Mechelen for the march, said: "I am here to show solidarity with the parents. What has happened in the last few weeks moved me greatly. The system must become more humane."

The marchers, who included large numbers of parents with their children, adopted white as a symbol of hope, turning the three km (two mile) march route between North and South stations into a sea of white balloons bobbing in a chill wind.
At South station most demonstrators laid their flowers in front of billboard-size placards with 15 names of the dead girls and others suspected of having fallen into the hands of criminals.
The parents and relatives of the dead and missing girls later met Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene at his official residence.
Dehaene said afterwards he had made four promises, including the creation of an independent national centre for missing and exploited children before the end of the year

To try to sweep aside popular allegations of cover-up attempts by the authorities, he pledged everything would be done to ensure the investigation into the deaths of the four girls would be thorough and the truth would be brought to light.
He reiterated that he would urge parliament to remove an article from the Belgian constitution which states that all political parties should be represented on the judiciary.

The article is at the root of a system of political appointments, widely denounced as having created a network of justice officials who are sometimes more eager to protect friends than to carry out unbiased investigations.
